newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU proposes help to towns hit by Clabecq bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: EU proposes help to towns hit by Clabecq bankruptcy.

text.p: The European Commission proposed on Friday ways to help Belgium's Walloon region overcome difficulties caused by the bankruptcy of steel maker Clabecq -- a month after it rejected a regional rescue plan for the firm.

European Union Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies wrote a letter to Walloon Government President Robert Collignon listing measures on how the bloc's structural aid funds could be used to assist the two affected towns.
Commission spokeswoman Heike Gerstbrein told reporters the region had "enormous problems" because of the bankruptcy.
In her letter, Wulf-Mathies said the towns of Tubize and Rebecq could be included in a list of areas eligible for so called "Objective 2" EU aid in 1997-1999 for declining industrial regions.

However, the EU executive did not offer any extra funds for the country as a whole as the total amount of this kind of aid to Belgium would remain unchanged at a maximum of 114 million European currency units ($140.5 million) for the period.
"That means that some other region or part of another region would have to be taken out of the framework," Gerstbrein said.
Aid to the two towns could be used for diversification, training or to help small and medium-sized firms, she said.
Another possibility for assistance was through four so called EU Community Initiatives which are currently in operation in Wallonia.

Clabecq filed for bankruptcy in mid-December after the EU executive rejected a 1.5 billion Belgian franc ($47 million) rescue plan by the Walloon Region, which then withdrew its support from the firm.
A Belgian court declared loss-making Clabecq bankrupt on January 3 and appointed four receivers to run the company which has a full order book for at least this quarter.
Receivers have proposed re-employing about 1,400 of the 1,800-strong workforce.
Belgian radio said most of the remainder would be given early retirement. -- Brussels newsroom +32 2 287 68 11
